b.bio: William Ames (Latinized Guilielmus Amesius) was an English Puritan theologian and Ramist logician educated at Christ's College, Cambridge, under William Perkins. Driven from England by Laudian conformity pressures, he settled in the Netherlands, served as an anti-Arminian counselor at the Synod of Dort (1618–1619), and became professor of theology at Franeker, where he shaped a generation of Reformed and Puritan students. His thought wedded a sharply practical, conscience-oriented divinity to Ramist method, defining theology as "the doctrine of living to God." He polemicized vigorously against Roman Catholic controversialists—above all Robert Bellarmine—and against the Remonstrants. His writings shaped English congregationalism and New England Puritanism, where his systematic and casuistical works became standard texts. b.bio: Walter (Galterius cancellarius) was a French or Norman cleric who served as chancellor of Antioch under Roger of Salerno, roughly 1114 to 1122. He is known only through two self-references in his own work; he is not recorded in any charter or witness list, and his place of origin is disputed on grounds of gallicisms in his Latin versus his allegiance to the Norman Roger of Salerno. He was present at the Battle of Ager Sanguinis in 1119, where Ilghazi defeated and killed Roger, and was probably held briefly captive in Aleppo, an experience behind his harrowing account of prisoners' tortures, mutilations and executions.
b.s: The library holds his Bella Antiochena (Antiochian Wars), an eyewitness history of the principality's campaigns against Bursuq of Hamadan in 1115 and its disastrous defeat by Ilghazi of Aleppo in 1119, written with the explicit intent to demonstrate the workings of divine will through victory and disaster.

b.bio: Galterius Saveyr (Galterius Meldensis Episcopus, 'Sayer') was a late eleventh-century bishop of Meaux whose dated writings fall between 1071 and 1082, an era overlapping Gregory VII's pontificate. The works held under his name fit that setting: an epistle to Bartholomew attacking a simoniac abbot of Mont Saint-Michel in periculo maris, citing Gregory VII and the Cluniac church, and holding that invincible ignorance excuses association with simony while monks lack canonical license to preach or take penitents; and a life of the confessor Anastasius, which treats the sign of the cross against demons and dying in obedience. A different Walter — Gualterus de Castellione, the twelfth-century poet of the Alexandreis — is a separate person and is not this author.
b.s: His epistle is a witness to Gregorian-era conflict over simony and monastic jurisdiction, and his life of Anastasius to eleventh-century hagiography.

b.bio: the surviving records describe other twelfth-century Walters — Walter of Compiègne, Walter of Saint Victor, and Walter of Châtillon — none of whom matches this author (a monk of Cluny writing on Marian miracles), so they are disregarded as evidence about him. The library record shows a Gualterus, monk of Cluny, author of a short Latin work on the miracles of the Blessed Virgin Mary, printed in PL 173. In it he cites Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres and legate of the apostolic see, and defends miracle narratives against those who would dismiss them as vain and frivolous.
b.s: His single held work is a defense of Marian miracle stories, arguing that images may work miracles by divine power, that the Ave Maria derives from Gabriel's annunciation and protects even great sinners from divine vengeance, and that such narratives edify rather than amuse.

b.bio: Guarin (Garin, Guarinus) was abbot of the abbey of Saint-Victor in Paris and died in 1194; sources give no birth date. He is not to be confused with Garnier de Saint-Victor, the Victorine sub-prior of 1140 who died in 1170 and wrote the Gregorianum printed in PL 193. The letters held here are administrative and disciplinary correspondence from his abbacy: they concern papal confirmation of an abbatial election and resignation, disputes with Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, with the archbishop of Lund, with John, count of Eu, and a defense of the Grandmontines against their persecutors.
b.s: His surviving letters show a twelfth-century abbey head operating through papal authority—appeals to Alexander III, legatine intervention (legates Theoderic and Alexander), and canonical argument—in conflicts over jurisdiction, monastic custom, and promises extorted by deceit.

b.bio: William of Apulia wrote in the 1090s; nothing is known of his life except his name. He was probably a layman, based on the relative lack of religious references in his work. Wolf argues he was a Lombard rather than a Norman, given his sympathetic treatment of Lombard characters; Brown suggests he was born to Greek-speaking Lombard parents, noting his sympathetic treatment of Byzantines and his familiarity with the Byzantine court. He dedicated his poem to Roger Borsa and was probably a member of his court. The Gesta Roberti Wiscardi consists of 2,833 hexameters in five books with prologue and epilogue, composed between 1096 and 1099: the prologue addresses Urban II (died July 1099), and Book III refers to the First Crusade already underway.
b.s: His Gesta Roberti Wiscardi is one of the principal contemporary sources for the Norman conquest of southern Italy and the only epic-historical poem dealing with that conquest, covering the Normans' arrival in southern Italy through Robert Guiscard's Balkan campaigns against the Byzantines (1081–85).

b.bio: Guillelmus Dandina is known only through two works printed in PL 204, both dated to 1157 in Migne's Patrologia Latina: a life of Hugh of Lacerta, institutor of the Grandmontine order, and an account of the travels of the Grandmontine brothers. The sources give no dates or places for his own life. His subject matter marks him as a writer within or close to the Grandmontine order in twelfth-century France.
b.s: His two surviving works are early hagiographic and historical sources for the Grandmontine order and its founder Hugh of Lacerta; the Vita presents Hugh as pre-elected by divine grace from infancy and as practicing voluntary poverty and perfect abstinence.

b.bio: William the Walloon, printed here as William of Saint-Arnould of Metz, became abbot of St. Arnoul at Metz in 1050. In 1073 he was elected abbot of St-Remi in Reims, but Archbishop Manasses of Reims persecuted him despite promises made in person, and William journeyed to Rome to secure the acceptance of his resignation from St-Remi. Gregory VII wrote on his behalf to both Manasses and Bishop Herimann of Metz. In 1085 William was consecrated bishop of Metz, resigned within a year, retired to Gorze, and was later restored to St. Arnoul by Herimann. His letters include an address congratulating Gregory VII on his election.
b.s: The works held here are his seven letters and an oration in commemoration of St. Augustine: polemical and exhortatory texts chiefly against Archbishop Manasses of Reims, arguing that moral fitness must precede exercise of canonical power and that good and bad are separated in heart rather than body.

b.bio: William of Volpiano, called of Saint-Bénigne or Dijon, was born on the island of San Giulio in Lake Orta, Piedmont, son of Count Robert of Volpiano. Oblate at Locedio near Vercelli, he joined Cluny under Abbot Majolus in 987 and was elected abbot of Saint-Bénigne at Dijon in 990, being ordained priest the same year by Bruno, bishop of Dijon. He led the Cluniac reform across Burgundy, Normandy, and Lorraine, ruling over more than forty monasteries, founded Fruttuaria in Lombardy (1001–03) with help from his brothers and his uncle King Arduin of Italy, and reformed Fécamp, Jumièges, and Mont Saint-Michel. He died at Fécamp on 1 January 1031.
b.s: The works held here are his letters and charters defending Fruttuaria's exemption from episcopal and secular subjection — documents of the eleventh-century struggle for monastic liberty against the bishop of Autun.

b.bio: William V, called William the Great, was duke of Aquitaine and count of Poitou from 990 until his death on 31 January 1030. Born at Poitiers in 969, son of William IV and Emma of Blois, he was well educated, a collector of books, and a friend and correspondent of Bishop Fulbert of Chartres; he turned his court into a centre of learning in southern France. Upon the death of the emperor Henry II he was offered the kingdom of Italy but declined to contest it against Conrad II. The works held here are not theology but letters and a diploma: correspondence touching church affairs (undertakings proceeding only with episcopal consent, deposing bishops to gain a kingdom as sin, monastic reform by importing observant monks) and a diploma concerning the village of St. Macarius.
b.s: He matters to readers of this shelf as a lay ruler whose surviving letters document how royal power negotiated with bishops and monasteries around the year 1000.

b.bio: Born at Champeaux near Melun around 1070, William studied under Anselm of Laon and Roscelin, taught at the cathedral school of Notre-Dame in Paris, becoming head of the school and archdeacon of Paris around 1100–1103, and retired to St Victor in 1108 amid disputes with his pupil Abelard over his realist doctrine of universals. He became Bishop of Châlons-sur-Marne in 1114. Most of what is recorded of him comes through Abelard, who was hostile.
b.s: The library holds a charter on parochial rights, tithes, burial, vows, and excommunication, and a short treatise defending that Christ is whole under each species of the altar against those requiring communion in both kinds—documents of his episcopal administration at Châlons rather than his better-known logical writings.

b.bio: Guillelmus de Trahinaco appears in the sources only as a prior assigned by Migne's Patrologia Latina to the years 1150–1200. The entry under his name in PL 204 (cols. 1177–1178B) consists of a brief life and list of works drawn from Gallia Christiana; no dates of birth or death, no religious order, and no see or abbey are given there. He should not be confused with the later French canonist Guillaume Durand, Bishop of Mende (c. 1230 – 1 November 1296), who shares the Latinized name William but belongs to the thirteenth century and wrote on canon law and liturgy.
b.s: The library holds letters printed under his name in PL 204; beyond that volume's brief Gallia Christiana notice, the record offers little to identify him further.

w: Charter for the Church of Liège

b.bio: Wazo was bishop of Liège from 1041 until his death in 1048, having earlier served as scholaster of the cathedral school under Notker of Liège, under whom he had studied alongside Heriger of Lobbes. His election as bishop was contested, with Emperor Henry III against him. As a temporal prince he took part in imperial politics but challenged the emperor's caesaropapist tendencies, notably at the deposition of Pope Gregory VI by the Council of Sutri in 1046, where he held that the pope may be judged by no one but God. His life was chronicled by his contemporary Anselm of Liège.
b.s: The works held here are a charter for the church of Liège and letters; the charter is dated by incarnation year and indiction. Wazo is also known for his letter to Roger of Châlons on heresy, which argued via the Parable of the Tares that the church should tolerate dissent rather than shed blood.

b.bio: Wulfad was ordained a priest by Ebbo of Reims during Ebbo's second incumbency, and served as abbot of Montier-en-Der from 856 and of Soissons from 858, tutoring Carloman, son of Charles the Bald. He may have acted as notary for the anti-king Pippin II of Aquitaine in 847–48; in 859 the synod of Savonnières removed him from priestly office with the other Ebbo ordinands. Charles the Bald nonetheless appointed him archbishop of Bourges in 866 over Hincmar's objections to his eligibility, and in 868 secured papal recognition.
b.s: The library holds a single short pastoral letter (PL 121) treating sin, penance and confession, sacraments, lawful oaths, obedience to rulers, and the honor due priests — a compact specimen of Carolingian pastoral instruction.

b.bio: Waldram (also Walthram) was a monk of St. Gall, first attested in documents in 885, serving as subdeacon from about 895 and deacon from 902. He held the office of librarian of the abbey from 905 to 909, succeeding Notker Balbulus (succeeded by Werinher), and worked as a charter scribe. He composed three poems to Dado of Verdun in 906, a greeting poem for King Conrad I in 911, and two hymns. He died on a 14 November, after 926.
b.s: The library holds his Latin poems (PL 132); he is a minor figure among the verse productions associated with the St. Gall scriptorium.

w: Letter to the Church of Bamberg

b.bio: The library's record shows an eleventh-century Latin author writing against King Henry IV and the Gregorian reformers, defending divinely ordained rulers and canonical satisfaction under pain of excommunication, and corresponding with Saint Anselm. The surviving records do not describe this man: they cover Durandus of Troarn, Robert de Neubourg, and Waleran de Beaumont, Count of Meulan (1104–1166) — different persons sharing the name or place, and none can be credited with these works.
b.s: His held works are Investiture-era polemic and hagiography: a life of Leonard, letters to Bamberg, to Louis, to Anselm, and an epistle arguing for obedience to ordained rulers against Henry IV and the papal party.

b.bio: Walter was bishop of Orléans from 867 to 892, active in late Carolingian West Francia. A recent master's thesis on his career shows he governed the diocese through a capitulary promulgated in the second year of his tenure and acted as a political broker in Neustria, associated with Hugh the Abbot and later supporting Odo, the first non-Carolingian king of West Francia. The work held here is that capitulary: a set of chapters citing Carolingian capitalaries, Herard of Tours, Nicaea, Hincmar, and Theodulf, ordering archdeacons to examine priests' faith and masses, requiring right faith and catholic baptism of priests, forbidding clergy to bear arms, directing bishops to examine clerics before ordination, and stating doctrine on the Trinity, the incarnation, judgment, resurrection, and eternal reward or punishment.
b.s: His capitulary is a working document of ninth-century diocesan reform and clerical discipline, showing how a Carolingian bishop enforced orthodoxy and sacramental order locally.

b.bio: This Walter is not to be confused with the twelfth-century poet Walter of Châtillon (Gualterus de Castellione), author of the Alexandreis; the library's single item under this name belongs to a different shelf and corpus. The library's item is a set of diplomas in PL 160 in which Walter appears as bishop of the church of Chalon, acting alongside Savericus, count of Chalon, Geoffrey of Dunzy, and Gocerannus (Jocerannus), bishop of Langres. The documents record a pledge of revenues by the count to the church, secured by hostages under oath of peace, with provisions for breach of pact.
b.s: The diplomas here are legal-historical records of episcopal-countly relations: church property pledged against lay power, monasteries freed from lay control, and a stricter Benedictine observance justifying a new foundation.

b.bio: Walter of Sens was a Frankish archbishop who held the see of Sens from 887 until his death in November 923. He crowned three kings at St-Medard's Abbey in Soissons: Eudes in 888, Robert I in July 922, and Rudolph on 13 July 923. He inherited from his uncle Walter, Bishop of Orléans, a Carolingian sacramentary composed for St-Amand between 855 and 873, which he gave to the church of Sens. The statutes printed under his name in PL 132 are disciplinary canons: they regulate monastic common life in refectory and dormitory, restrict nuns' movements and property dealings without episcopal license, reserve general excommunication for grave excess, and require assiduous celebration of divine service.
b.s: The single work held here is a set of disciplinary statutes showing how a ninth-century metropolitan legislated for monks, nuns, and parish clergy under his jurisdiction.

w: History of the Translation of SS. Chrysanthus and Daria
On the Creation of the World
On the Miracles of St. Goar
On the Names of the Twelve Months
Text of the following metrical work

b.bio: Wandalbert of Prüm, born in 813, was a Benedictine monk and theological writer. He was apparently a native of Francia and by 839 was a monk at Prüm, where Abbot Markward commissioned him to rewrite the old life of St. Goar and add an account of the saint's miracles. At the request of Otrich, a priest of Cologne, and with the aid of his friend Florus of Lyons, he composed a martyrology in verse, finished about 848, based chiefly on Bede's martyrology and arranged by calendar day. With the martyrology stand poems on the months, agricultural labors, hunting and fishing seasons, and the church Hours; he also wrote a work on the Mass, now lost.
b.s: His verse martyrology is one of the principal Carolingian reworkings of Bede's calendar, and his Life and Miracles of St. Goar preserve early testimony to a Rhineland cult centered on healing at a saint's memorial.

b.bio: Warnaharius is known only as a priest (presbyter) of the church of Langres who wrote saints' lives. The Lexikon des Mittelalters places him as a cleric of Langres in the first half of the seventh century; CERL and Deutsche Biographie give 'around 614' as his date, while Biblissima records a broad not-before-501 / not-after-699 span. He composed a letter to Ceraunius, bishop of Paris, and two passiones: that of the Tergemini brothers Speusippus, Eleusippus and Meleusippus, martyrs under Aurelian, and that of Desiderius, bishop at Langres.
b.s: His two passiones here are early Merovingian martyr narratives presenting martyrdom as wrought by love of faith and divine predestination, against pagan idolaters.

b.bio: Wilhelm Wattenbach (born Rantzau, Holstein, 22 September 1819; died Frankfurt, 20 September 1897) was a German historian. He studied philology at Bonn, Göttingen and Berlin, joined the Monumenta Germaniae Historica in 1843, became archivist at Breslau in 1855, professor at Heidelberg in 1862 and at Berlin in 1873, where he sat on the MGH central directorate from 1875 and chaired it 1886–88. His principal work was Deutschlands Geschichtsquellen im Mittelalter bis zur Mitte des XIII Jahrhunderts (1858), a guide to medieval German sources; he also wrote manuals of Greek and Latin palaeography and Das Schriftwesen im Mittelalter.
b.s: The works held here are not patristic texts but Wattenbach's editorial apparatus for Migne's Patrologia Latina: a notice on Arnulf (PL 147) and prolegomena to a volume (PL 154), reflecting his expertise in identifying and dating medieval documents.

b.bio: Guibert (or Wibert) was born at Parma between about 1020 and 1030 to a noble family related to the counts/margraves of Canossa (one source gives Ravenna, c. 1029). He served as imperial chancellor for Italy under Empress Agnes from 1057/58 until 1063, backed the antipope Honorius II (Cadalus of Parma), and in 1072 King Henry IV named him bishop/archbishop of Ravenna. Elected pope by the pro-imperial Synod of Brixen on 25 June 1080 against Gregory VII, he took the name Clement III and was consecrated in Rome in March 1084. He died at Civita Castellana on 8 September 1100.
b.s: The letters and privileges held here are chancery documents of his rival papacy, asserting papal privilege over church property, interim investiture authority for provosts, precedence for the archbishop of Ravenna, and voiding forged documents — polemic aimed at Gregory VII's party, the schismatics, Milanese and Aquileian rivals, and Duke Wratislaus I of Bohemia.

b.bio: Wibold, a native of Cambrai from a prominent local family, was archdeacon of Noyon with authority to discipline clergy before his election as bishop of Cambrai. Invested by Emperor Otto the Great in 971 after a journey to Italy, he died after about a year in office, his health broken by the trip. He bequeathed a deluxe gospel book and other volumes to the cathedral of Cambrai. The Deeds of the Bishops of Cambrai preserves his own account of the ludus regularis seu clericalis, a dice game with virtues in place of stakes, devised to keep clerics from gambling.
b.s: The work held here is the text of the ludus regularis, a moralizing dice game pairing virtues and vices so that clergy might overcome vice through charity instead of secular dicing.

b.bio: Widric of Saint-Ghislain was abbot of the monastery of Saint-Ghislain in Hainaut, attested by a single letter dated 1065 addressed to Emperor Henry III. The letter defends his monastery against Count Baldwin, arguing that royal liberty shields monastic churches from secular seizure, that the prince bears the sword to defend the oppressed, and that the emperor will answer at the last judgment for failing justice. He is not to be confused with Widricus, abbot of Saint-Evre at Toul, a separate eleventh-century figure.
b.s: His surviving letter is a mid-eleventh-century witness to monastic claims of liberty and protection under imperial justice, written against Count Baldwin's encroachments.

b.bio: A Saxon monk of Corvey, admitted to the monastery during the abbacy of Folcmar (917–942); the only external witness to him is that entry list. Almost everything else known of him comes from his own work: the Res gestae Saxonicae in three books, begun in 967 and dedicated to Mathilde, Abbess of Quedlinburg. He also wrote lives of St. Paul the Hermit and St. Thecla, now lost.
b.s: His Deeds of the Saxons is often the sole authority for events of Henry I's and Otto I's reigns and a primary source for tenth-century Germany under the Ottonians. He imitates classical writers, especially Sallust. Although not a member of the royal court, he was extremely well informed about imperial politics, probably through imperial officers visiting Corvey.

b.bio: Wigo headed the Benedictine monastery at Feuchtwangen in Franconia in the closing decades of the tenth century. The letters preserved under his name are addressed chiefly to Bishop Liutold of Augsburg (988–996), thanking him for aid and reporting the monastery's troubles with a violent local lord, the son of Richard (Rihhardi), and hostile neighbors. Gustav Bossert edited the letters as a source for the history of the Württemberg Franconia region.
b.s: His surviving letters document the dependence of a small Ottonian monastery on episcopal protection against lay violence, and are a primary source for regional history.

b.bio: William of Æbelholt (also William of Paris or of Eskilsø) was born in Paris around 1125 to a noble French family, educated by his uncle Hugh, abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and received a prebend at Sainte-Geneviève-du-Mont before being presented to the priory of Épinay. He came to Denmark around 1165 to reform the Augustinian community on Eskilsø; about ten years later the house moved to Æbelholt, which became the largest Augustinian house in Scandinavia. He died on Easter Sunday (6 April) 1203 and was canonized by Pope Honorius III in 1224 after an inquiry entrusted to Archbishop Anders Sunesen of Lund. The library holds two pages from PL 209: prolegomena material on theological method accompanying his letters.
b.s: The works here are letters whose preface argues that labor for the neighbor's common utility pleases God, that such writings are destined for the unlearned rather than the learned, that the names of bishops lend letters greater authority, and that their solutions contain nothing beyond the saints' sanction.

b.bio: William of Hirsau was a Benedictine abbot and monastic reformer, born in Bavaria around 1030 and educated as a puer oblatus at St. Emmeram's Abbey in Regensburg, where Otloh of St. Emmeram taught him. Called to Hirsau in 1069 to succeed the deposed Abbot Frederick, he declined abbatial benediction until Frederick's death in 1071. He rebuilt Hirsau on Cluniac lines, introduced lay brothers into German Benedictine monasteries, obtained papal exemption from Gregory VII in 1075, and supported the pope against Henry IV in the Investiture Controversy. He died at Hirsau on 5 July 1091; Britannica gives 2 July. He is honored as a Blessed in the Catholic Church.
b.s: The works held here are the Constitutiones Hirsaugienses, the rulebook of the Hirsau Reforms that shaped German monasticism, together with his treatise on music (built on Guido and Boethius, holding that the operation of the principal strings governs all modal theory) and a preface to his astronomical works.

b.bio: William of St. Thomas of the Paraclete (c. 1125–1203) — The library prints this name for William of Paris, usually called William of Æbelholt or William of Eskilsø. Born in Paris around 1125 to a noble French family and educated by his uncle Hugh, abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, he held a canonry at Sainte-Geneviève-du-Mont and became sub-prior when Victorine canons regular took over that house in 1148. In 1161 Absalon, bishop of Roskilde, recruited canons regular from Paris to reform the monastery of St. Thomas on Eskilsø in Denmark; William became abbot there and moved the community to Æbelholt, where he died on Easter Sunday, 1203, and was buried. He was canonized in 1224 by Pope Honorius III.
b.s: The works here are not doctrinal treatises but historical documents gathered under his name: a genealogy tracing Queen Ingeborg of France to the Danish kings against Flemish claims, diplomatic acts, an account of the revelation of the relics of Saint Genevieve, and the instrument founding Absalon's anniversary.

b.bio: William of Auvergne (Guilielmus Alvernus), born at Aurillac, became master of theology at the University of Paris in 1223 and professor by 1225, and served as Bishop of Paris from 1228 until his death in 1249. He defended the mendicant orders against secular clergy attacks and was among the first Latin thinkers to engage Aristotle and Arabic philosophy critically against Christian doctrine. Note on attribution: the single work this library holds under his name, a short 'Testament' printed in PL 133, argues for donations to Peter and Paul, almsgiving benefiting souls, free abbatial election without lay control, and papal protection for Benedictine monasteries — material that reads like an early medieval charter rather than the bishop's known scholastic corpus, so its attribution should be treated with caution.
b.s: The first major Latin theologian to confront Aristotelian and Islamic philosophy systematically; the 'Testament' held here, if his, documents episcopal piety and monastic reform rather than doctrine.

b.bio: A Norman Benedictine monk of Jumièges, known almost entirely through his dedicatory letter to William the Conqueror and his nickname 'Calculus' (per Orderic Vitalis). He was an eyewitness of some events under Duke Richard III (1026–7), which suggests a birth around 1000. His death after 1070 is unrecorded, though the Catholic Encyclopedia places it at Jumièges about 1090. Around 1070 he compiled the Gesta Normannorum Ducum, reworking Dudo of Saint-Quentin's earlier history of the Norman dukes, correcting its exaggerations, and carrying the narrative down to 1087 in seven books of his own.
b.s: His Gesta Normannorum Ducum is one of the earliest histories of the Norman dukes and one of the first accounts of the conquest of England, written from a Norman point of view by a contemporary of 1066.

w: 6th Life of St. Thomas of Canterbury

b.bio: William of Canterbury was a Benedictine monk of Christ Church Priory, ordained deacon by Thomas Becket in 1170 and present at the archbishop's murder that December; he admitted in his writings that he fled the scene. He wrote one of the five lives of Becket composed at Canterbury soon after the martyrdom, and later collected miracle stories about him. His hagiography was used by later medieval writers on Becket.
b.s: His Life of St Thomas is a primary witness to Becket's conflict with Henry II over the church's liberty, written by an eyewitness of the murder.

w: Speech to his army before the battle
The Words of William the Conqueror on His Deathbed

b.bio: William the Conqueror, Duke of Normandy from 1035 and first Norman King of England from 1066 until his death on 9 September 1087, is the author named here. The library holds not his writings in a literary sense but the documentary record attached to his name: laws, diplomas confirming grants to monasteries, letters, a speech to his army before battle, and a text of his deathbed words. The legal material treats royal confirmation of ecclesiastical gifts, exemption of monasteries from episcopal jurisdiction by royal privilege, fines such as hengwite for taking a thief without hue and cry, and penalties of forty shillings for self-help justice without royal license.
b.s: These PL 149 documents show how royal law and privilege shaped the English church after 1066; readers of the Laws and Diplomas see the king acting as guarantor of monastic rights against both local claimants and episcopal jurisdiction.

b.bio: A Norman priest born at Préaux near Pont-Audemer to a knightly family, William trained first as a soldier, then studied at Poitiers and took orders around 1049. He became chaplain to Duke William of Normandy and, by Orderic Vitalis's account, archdeacon of Lisieux; he does not appear in surviving charters, so some details rest on Orderic alone. His Gesta Willelmi ducis Normannorum et regis Anglorum, written between 1071 and 1077, covers roughly 1047–1068 (the opening and close are lost) and was used by Orderic. He also wrote verses.
b.s: His Gesta is the fullest contemporary Norman account of the Conquest, openly partisan: it argues Edward designated William heir, that Harold was a perjured usurper, and that the good ruler protects churches and the powerless — theses the library's pages assert against Harold, Archbishop Malger, and Guy of Arques.

b.bio: None of The surviving records describes this William of Reims: they treat William of Saint-Thierry (d. 1148) and William of Jumièges, different men whose works do not match the library's holdings. The library record is therefore the only evidence. Its four items — diplomas, a dedicatory letter to a William, general letters, and a letter to Peter the Chanter — sit in PL 205 and PL 209 among Reims material, dispute with the chapter of Reims and with Henri de France, and cite the Reims historians Marlot and Varin heavily. This points plausibly toward William of the White Hands, archbishop of Reims, but no source confirms it.
b.s: The works held are administrative and polemical documents connected with the see of Reims: diplomas on liberties, judgments, and penitential relaxation, argued against the cathedral chapter of Reims and against Henri de France.

b.bio: An Anglo-Saxon priest from Wessex living at Mainz, commissioned by Archbishop Lullus and Bishop Megingoz of Würzburg to write a life of the recently dead missionary Boniface. He had never met Boniface but interviewed those who had. Some scholars identify him with Willibald of Eichstätt, Boniface's kinsman and first bishop of that see; the identification is debated and unproven. His Latin is an Anglo-Latin style modelled on Aldhelm, drawing on Pseudo-Hegesippus, Eusebius of Caesarea, and Gregory the Great's Dialogues.
b.s: His Vita Bonifatii (written probably between 763 and 768) is the earliest known biography from the Germanic-speaking world and the source for Boniface's felling of the Oak of Jupiter.

w: Verses for the Death of Conrad

b.bio: Wipo, also spelled Wippo and perhaps originally named Wigbert, was a priest, poet, and chronicler of the first half of the eleventh century, apparently a native of Burgundy. He served as chaplain to Emperor Conrad II and may have acted as tutor to Conrad's son Henry III, to whom he presented his biography of the emperor in 1046 not long after Henry's coronation. His writings draw on the Vulgate and classical Latin authors; he does not cite patristic texts. The Easter sequence Victimae paschali laudes is often attributed to him, though on uncertain grounds.
b.s: His Gesta Chuonradi II imperatoris is a key source for Conrad II's reign, and the works held here treat kingship as divinely appointed for the church's good and argue that recording princes' deeds incites virtue in posterity.

w: Prefaces to his books on the acts of the Saints

b.bio: Wolfhard, a monk and priest at Herrieden in the late ninth century, is attested in sources from 882 and died around 900–902. He wrote hagiographical works on Saint Walpurga, abbess of Heidenheim: a prose Life (dated 893), prefatory material to his books on the acts of the Saints, and a poem on Walpurga. The library prints his name as Wolfhard of Hasenried; sources also give him as Wolfhardus Hasenrietanus or monachus Haserensis. His works defend miracle reports against skeptics and mockers, attributing healing miracles to grace rather than human merit.
b.s: His Vita Sancti Walpurgis is the principal ninth-century account of the Heidenheim abbess, arguing that saints intercede for bodily healings and that persevering prayer obtains what it asks.

w: On the Sacrament of the Altar

b.bio: Wolfhelm (Wolphelm) of Brauweiler was a Benedictine monk who was educated and taught at the cathedral school of Cologne, entered the Benedictine order at the reform monastery of St. Maximin in Trier in 1036, and became the third abbot of Brauweiler in 1065. He died on 22 April 1091 at Brauweiler. He wrote against Berengar of Tours in the eucharistic controversy, addressing a letter to Meginhard of Gladbach Abbey. Manegold of Lautenbach attacked him in the Liber contra Wolfelmum, accusing him of mediating between Macrobius's Platonism and Christian doctrine and denying the Antipodes; Wolfhelm's closeness to Emperor Henry IV gave the attack a political edge. A hagiographical Vita by the Brauweiler monk Konrad was written around 1115.
b.s: He is remembered chiefly as the target of Manegold's Liber contra Wolfelmum and as an opponent of Berengar of Tours; the works held here are his treatise On the Sacrament of the Altar and his Verses on Both Testaments.

b.bio: Wulfstan the Cantor, also known as Wulfstan of Winchester, was an Anglo-Saxon monk of the Old Minster at Winchester. His birth date is unknown, but personal references in his poem Narratio metrica de S. Swithuno suggest he was a child at St Swithun's canonization in 971, leading scholars to believe he was born about 960 and given as a child to the Old Minster, where he spent his mature life. He studied under Bishop Æthelwold of Winchester, became a monk and a priest, then rose to become precentor, responsible for leading chant, recruiting and training the choir, and composing poems and hymns; he also worked as a scribe and hagiographer. The day of his death, 22 July, is recorded in a New Minster calendar without the year; his latest datable work is the Vita S. Aethelwoldi, composed no earlier than 996, so he presumably died in the early 11th century.
b.s: The works held here are his Vita S. Aethelwoldi, an account of Æthelwold's restoration of monasteries replacing clerics with monks (and noting that the English church commemorated Æthelwold since his death), and a letter to Alphege (Ælfheah) treating prayer, the saints' vision of God, and the state of elect souls gathered where Christ is until resurrection.
